draft.title: Traditional and behavioural economics
card: Traditional economics assumes people are rational, well informed and self-interested. They weigh costs and benefits and choose what gives them the most satisfaction.
Behavioural economics studies how people actually decide. It uses experiments and observation to test the traditional assumptions.
These studies often find that people act in ways the traditional model does not predict. They may rely on mental shortcuts, lack full information or care about others.
Behavioural economics does not throw out traditional economics. It adds evidence about real behaviour to make predictions more accurate.
draft.remember: Traditional economics assumes rational choosers. Behavioural economics tests that with evidence.

a.q: Which statement best describes the traditional economic view of a consumer?
opts: A well informed person who acts in their own interest
A person who often follows mental shortcuts when choosing
A person who mainly aims to be fair to other people
A person who gets most choices wrong without experiments
a.why: Traditional economics assumes people are rational, informed and self-interested. The other options describe findings of behavioural economics, which tests those assumptions.
a.clue: Think about the three assumptions the traditional model makes.

b.q: Researchers in Geelong watch how 200 shoppers choose between brands and find many pick the first brand they see. What does this suggest?
opts: Real choices can differ from the rational choices predicted
People always choose the brand that is cheapest
Traditional economics has been proven wrong in every case
Shoppers in Geelong are not self-interested at all
b.why: The study observes real behaviour and finds it differs from the model of careful, informed choice. It does not show the model fails in every case, and it says nothing about shoppers being unselfish.
b.clue: Compare what the shoppers did with what a fully rational chooser would do.

a.best: A well informed person who acts in their own interest

b.best: Real choices can differ from the rational choices predicted

problems.detail: The right option is the only hedged one ('can differ'). Every distractor uses an absolute ('not ... at all', 'in every case', 'always'), so a student can pick the answer by spotting the qualifier without knowing the idea.

Why (a) says all the other options describe findings of behavioural economics. 'A person who gets most choices wrong without experiments' is not a behavioural finding, so the explanation misdescribes that distractor.

a.q: Which statement best describes the traditional economic view of a consumer?
opts: A well informed person who acts in their own interest
A person who often follows mental shortcuts when choosing
A person who mainly aims to be fair to other people
A person who rarely compares costs and benefits
a.why: Traditional economics assumes people are rational, informed and self-interested, so they weigh costs and benefits. The other three options describe people who depart from that model, which is the kind of behaviour the traditional view does not assume.
a.clue: Think about the three assumptions the traditional model makes.

b.q: Researchers in Geelong watch how 200 shoppers choose between brands and find many pick the first brand they see. What does this research best show?
opts: It tests a traditional assumption by observing real choices
It replaces traditional economics with a better model
It assumes shoppers weigh up all costs and benefits
It shows that shoppers care most about being fair
b.why: The researchers observe real behaviour to check whether people choose as the rational model predicts, which is what behavioural economics does. It does not replace traditional economics: it adds evidence to make predictions more accurate. Weighing all costs and benefits is the traditional assumption, not the finding.
b.clue: What were the researchers checking when they watched the shoppers?
